newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Serious crime rises sharply in Kazakhstan.
newsitem.headline: Serious crime rises sharply in Kazakhstan.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan, its streets blacked out at night to save energy and its population suffering economic hardships, is witnessing a sharp rise in serious crime, according to figures released on Thursday.

Maratkali Nukenov, deputy chairman of the State Investigation Committee, told a news conference that serious crimes had risen by nearly 50 percent in 1996 and accounted for more than 60 percent of all crimes in the Central Asian state.
"Our main concern is the growing number of premeditated murders and rapes," Nukenov said.
The number of crimes overall in Kazakhstan, a republic with a mixed population of mostly Kazakhs and Russians, reached 146,500 last year, or three percent less than in 1995.
Nunenov called the news conference amid rising public concern over serious crime in Kazakhstan since the murder of a 28-year-old U.S. journalist in the capital, Almaty.

Chris Gehring, who had been running a U.S. media charity in Kazakhstan, was found dead in his flat on January 9. The murder alarmed foreigners living in Kazakhstan and was widely reported in the local and foreign media.
Five days after the murder, police said they had detained three people, two of them drug addicts, and that they had confessed to killing Gehring.
Playing down the need for alarm, Nukenov said: "One should not whip up passions and concerns among our foreign guests, whose assistance to our country is much appreciated."
Despite this, Nukenov said five foreigners had been killed in Kazakhstan in 1996. He did not give their nationality.
Police blame "social hardships in the transition to a market economy" for the growth in serious crime in the country of nearly 17 million people.
Few people go out at night in Almaty, which has a population of about 1.5 million. Most street lights are switched off after nine p.m. (1400 GMT) to save electricity because of an energy crisis.
In an effort to crack down on crime, local television responded to a suggestion by President Nursultan Nazarbayev last year to show a criminal being executed by firing squad.
The footage disgusted many viewers and prompted protests by human rights activists.
